summary: Johann Bernoulli was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied at the University of Basel and served as a Mitglied at the Prussian Academy of Sciences from around 1764 to 1807.
Johann Christoph Adelung was a linguist who studied at the Kloster Berge school and the University of Halle-Wittenberg from circa 1752 to 1754.

Johann Gottfried Eichhorn worked in religious studies and history/archaeology. He studied at Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne (~1770–1774), was professor of Oriental languages at Jena (~1775–1788), and served as Professor of Philosophy at Göttingen (~1788–1827).

Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the University of Greifswald (~1808–1812). He held posts at the University of Jena (~1817–1824) and as professor at Greifswald (~1824–1850).

Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff, an Indologist, studied at the University of Tübingen (~1791–1797). He held posts at the Imperial University of Dorpat (~1803–1809), University of Würzburg (~1809–1817), and University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1818–1835).

Johanna Engelberta van Lohuizen-de Leeuw worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. After studying at Utrecht University (~1939–1949), she held posts at Groningen (~1950–1951) and directed the Institute of South Asian Archaeology at Amsterdam (1959–1983).

Johanna Narten specialized in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. She studied at Saarland University (~1951–1956) and held a post at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg from circa 1971 to 1993.

Johannes Beltz is a scholar of Indology and religious studies. He earned doctorates in 1999 from the University of Lausanne and the École Pratique des Hautes Études, supervised by Marie-Louise Reiniche and Johannes Bronkhorst.

Johannes Bronkhorst studied at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Savitribai Phule Pune University under Shivaram Dattatray Joshi (PhD ~1976–1979), and Leiden University (~1979–1980). A scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy, he became professor at Lausanne in 1987.

Johannes Gildemeister studied at Göttingen under Heinrich Ewald and at Bonn under Georg Wilhelm Freytag and Christian Lassen. He was professor on the theological faculty at Marburg (~1845–1859) and later professor at Bonn (~1859–1890) in Indology and linguistics.

Johannes Hertel studied at Leipzig University (PhD ~1891–1897). Specializing in Indology, he taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1920) and later held the chair for Indian philology at Leipzig University (~1920–1937), succeeding Ernst Windisch.

Johannes Klatt was an Indologist who studied under Albrecht Weber (~1869–1872) and at the University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1872–1873). He served as custos of the Indian department at the Berlin State Library (~1874–1892).

Johannes Nobel studied at Berlin (~1906–1911) under Heinrich Lüders. Active in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, he held a post at Berlin (~1921–1928) and served as professor at Marburg (~1928–1955), succeeding Karl Friedrich Geldner.

Johannes Rahder studied at Utrecht (~1915–1926). Specializing in Indology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies, he succeeded Willem Caland in 1929, held posts at Utrecht, Leiden (1931–1946), Hawaii (1946–1947), and served as professor at Yale (1961–1962).

Johannes Schmidt studied under August Schleicher at Jena and Albrecht Weber at Bonn. A linguist and Indologist, he held posts at Bonn (~1868–1873) and Graz (~1873–1876), before serving as professor at Berlin (~1876–1901).

Johannes Schneider works in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies. He has been affiliated with the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities (attested 2013) and served as an editorial board member at the Deshana Institute (attested 2021).

Johannes Schubert, a scholar of Tibetology and sinology, studied under August Conrady (~1922–1925) and August Hermann Francke. He held posts at the Ahnenerbe (~1939–1945) and served as professor of Tibetan at Leipzig University (~1952–1961).

John A. Ardussi specializes in Tibetology and history/archaeology. He completed an MA under Turrell V. Wylie, earned a PhD attested in 1977 from Australian National University, and served on a CNRS research team.
John A. Brinkman is a historian and archaeologist who held posts at the University of Chicago and served as professor at the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures from circa 1963 to 2005.

John Allan was an Indologist and historian. He studied at the University of Edinburgh (~1901–1906) and Leipzig University (~1906–1907), later serving as Keeper of the Department of Coins and Medals at the British Museum (~1931–1949).
